items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' — went straight from 'this is Joanna, how can I help?' into the transaction.

No agenda statement. She gave a partial roadmap ('I can just get some details about the move so I can provide you a more personalized estimate and then I can send everything in your email as well, okay?') but no 10-15 minute timeframe and no real 'sound good?' confirmation.
Never checked availability for the week of September 21 — asked when Patricia was planning to move, then never confirmed the calendar had room.
Home size never asked. She confirmed 'a house, is that right? Just one story' and stopped there — no square footage, no bedroom count at the destination.

BOX COUNT NEVER CAPTURED. Patricia said '...and then I got a [ton of] boxes' and Joanna's entire response was 'Mm-hmm.' On a pod unload the box count is the single largest driver of time and it is not in the file.
Walk distance never discussed at all. No question about pod-to-door distance, path, or driveway length — no school bus reference, no equivalent, nothing.

The heavy item was flagged by the customer and dropped by the rep. Patricia volunteered 'I have a love seat that's electric, so it is pretty heavy' and Joanna later asserted 'I don't think we have anything over 300 or 500 pounds from the list you've given me' without ever confirming the loveseat's weight or whether it comes apart.
Never asked about garage, storage unit, balcony, or additional rooms at the destination.
Never asked about additional stops.
Never asked the moving-stressor question — and this was a cross-country move from Oregon back to Texas, a genuine stress point the customer raised and the rep never acknowledged.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener.

HOURLY RATE MISSTATED: 'an hourly rate of $96 per hour per mover and typically... we always recommend two guys to help us out, so that's $100 per hour.' Two movers at $96 each is $192/hr, not $100/hr. The $690 total she landed on is built off $192/hr, so the total and the spoken rate do not reconcile.
Friday/Saturday rate never given — she named Sun-Thu as the lowest tier and said Fri/Sat 'is fine as well' without ever stating that price.
What's-included list incomplete: covered movers, taxes, insurance, credit card fees, disassembly and the truck, but never mentioned gas, wrap, pads, bands or tools.
Fumbled the price live on the call — quoted '$900', then 'let me just double-check sorry about that, one second', then '$690'. Also said 'the twenty a half hour minimum.'
15-minute prorated increments after the minimum never mentioned.
No sense-check anywhere — never asked 'does that make sense?' after pricing or after the clock explanation.
No typical time range given for the job. She jumped straight to 'I'm just estimating this move to be completed within the two and a half hour minimum' with no range and no upper bound.

Quote is not defensible for the job described: a full pod unload — electric loveseat, TV, TV stand, bookcase, table, end table, queen bed, wicker stand, printer stand, plant stands, plus an uncounted pile of boxes — priced at the bare 2.5 hour minimum, with no box count and no walk distance in the file.
Traffic never mentioned despite a South Austin to San Marcos leg.
Assembly/reassembly mentioned as included but never factored into the time — a queen bed coming out of a pod needs reassembly.

Save Your Ass prep speech entirely absent. Still applies on a pod unload: deciding which room each item goes to before the crew arrives, clearing the path from driveway to door, and taking small boxes in by hand all cut billable time.
Passive booking close — 'if you're ready to go ahead with the booking, just let us know when is your preferred date' instead of asking for the date on this call.
Never said 'any other questions before I let you go?'
Never gave hours or a direct number — only 'give us a call' for changes.
Never explained the bolded detail list at the top of the confirmation email or asked her to reply with corrections.
Used the customer's name only twice ('thank you so much and Patricia', 'rest assured Patricia') — needs 3+.
Insurance explanation was thin: '$2,000 coverage for any accidental damages' with no repair/replace/reimburse framing, no zero deductible, no 60 cents/lb baseline for contrast.
Stacked confirmation questions and answered them herself ('is that right? Okay, got it. Alright.') rather than pausing for real answers.
The realtor referral was surfaced and then wasted — Patricia named Latica Finley as the source and Joanna said 'I see, okay, thank you so much' and moved on.
top_strength: Two real strengths. First, she proactively volunteered the day-of-week pricing structure without being asked — 'if your dates are flexible... Sundays through Thursdays our lowest hourly rate for the week' — which is genuinely budget-conscious selling to a customer whose pod delivery date is still flexible. Second, and better, she closed with the sharpest competitive coaching in either call on this run: when Patricia said she was gathering other quotes, Joanna did not get defensive, she said 'as you check around, just check what are the other fees outside of their hourly rate. You mentioned credit card fees, taxes, already included in our pricing. Again the only one outside of it is just the one time travel fee.' That reframes a price shop into an apples-to-apples comparison Einstein wins on, and it is exactly the right instinct. She also hit all three differentiators in sequence — the $2,000 coverage, Meet Your Mover ('we don't take daily contract workers... we'll send you their names ahead of time'), and the On-Time Guarantee ('if we run late, we provide discounts by the end of the day') — and opened warmly with 'Of course! I'd be glad to help you out with that.'
coaching_note: LIVE BUSINESS RISK, two of them, both need checking today. (1) The rate as spoken does not match the total as quoted. Joanna said '$96 per hour per mover... so that's $100 per hour' — two movers is $192/hr, and the $690 total she gave is $192 x 2.5 hours plus the $210 travel fee. Patricia is shopping this quote right now with '$100 an hour' written on her notepad next to a $690 total that cannot be produced from it. Pull the EMMA record and the confirmation email and make sure both say $192/hr for two movers; if the email went out with a different number than she heard, that is a misquote to correct proactively. (2) The estimate is a textbook under-quote and feeds straight into the estimate-accuracy rock. A full pod unload with a heavy electric loveseat, a queen bed to reassemble, and an uncounted quantity of boxes was priced at the bare 2.5 hour minimum, with zero walk distance captured. This move will very likely run over and become a bad-surprise conversation. Now the coaching. The single highest-leverage fix is that Patricia handed you the whole inventory in her first breath and you answered it with four 'mm-hmm's. When she trailed off at 'and then I got a [ton of] boxes,' that was the moment: 'Patricia, let me stop you there — roughly how many boxes are we talking? And that electric loveseat, do you know if the base detaches?' Then: 'How far is the pod going to sit from your front door — think of it in school bus lengths.' Those three questions take ninety seconds and they are the difference between a 2.5 hour quote and an accurate one. Second priority: give a range, never a single number. 'For a pod unload with about twenty-five boxes and the furniture you described, two movers typically run two and a half to four hours, so budget $690 to $980 including the travel fee — you only pay for the time actually used, so if we finish early you pay less.' A range protects you and it protects her. Third, do the pricing math before you say it out loud — quoting $900, apologizing, and correcting to $690 mid-call cost you credibility with a customer who was already planning to comparison shop. Fourth, run the Save Your Ass speech even on unloads, and last, work the referral: 'Latica Finley sent you? She's great, we've taken good care of her clients' is free trust you left on the table.
phone_presence_notes: Warmth markers are present and sound natural ('Of course! I'd be glad to help you out', 'Rest assured Patricia', 'of course, understood, no worries') and the customer left friendly, but she talked through the customer's inventory with filler 'mm-hmm's, asked and answered her own confirmation questions, and never acknowledged that Patricia is moving cross-country from Oregon.

Also want to verify whether her stacked 'is that right? Okay, got it' confirmations got real verbal answers from Patricia or whether she was answering for the customer.
